description: 🚀 Team BLAST is a group of enthusiastic students passionate about space, science, and technology. We aim to use NASA's open data, AI, and programming to solve real-world challenges creatively. We welcome teammates skilled in Python, AI/ML, data analysis, web development, UI/UX, and space science. Beginners with curiosity, creativity, and a willingness to learn are welcome too! Join us to innovate, collaborate
summary:
MissionVerse is an interactive, web-based space mission design game and flight simulator developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Players step into the role of a NASA Flight Director to engineer custom spacecraft, balance vital mass and electrical budgets, select appropriate rocket boosters, calculate Hohmann transfer orbits, and execute real-time flight operations.

Our project addresses the challenge by transforming intricate aerospace mathematics into accessible, gamified systems thinking. Rather than relying on speculative arcade physics, MissionVerse incorporates genuine orbital mechanics (Keplerian orbits and the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation) and directly streams live telemetry from NASA Open APIs—including Near-Earth Asteroid tracking from NASA JPL NeoWs and deep-space imagery from NASA APOD. During flight, unexpected space weather anomalies (solar flares, micrometeorite strikes) demand tactical, science-versus-survival trade-offs.

MissionVerse is important because it democratizes astronautics for the Artemis Generation. By bridging rigorous NASA astrophysics with intuitive, tactile gameplay, it empowers students, educators, and citizen scientists worldwide to experience the real engineering trade-offs behind exploring our solar system.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

MissionVerse is an interactive, physics-grounded space mission design simulator that guides players through the end-to-end lifecycle of deep-space exploration:

  • Target & Mission Selection: Players choose from diverse mission architectures (e.g., Earth Climate Sentinel in LEO, Lunar Gateway Relay, Mars Sample Return, Europa Ocean Explorer, or Near-Earth Asteroid Rendezvous).
  • Spacecraft Engineering Studio: Players assemble modular spacecraft subsystems (propulsion, solar arrays vs. RTGs, batteries, communication dishes, and scientific instrumentation). Subsystems actively calculate structural mass, power consumption, and delta-v capacity in real time.
  • Launch Vehicle Staging: Players match spacecraft wet mass against commercial and heavy-lift booster performance envelopes (Electron, Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, SLS/Starship).
  • Orbital Trajectory Planner: Users configure Hohmann transfer trajectories using an interactive scrubber that visualizes parking orbits, burn nodes, and arrival capture velocity while calculating required delta-v (Δv\Delta vΔv) via Keplerian physics and the Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation: Δv=Isp⋅g0⋅ln⁡(minitialmfinal)\Delta v = I_{\text{sp}} \cdot g_0 \cdot \ln\left(\frac{m_{\text{initial}}}{m_{\text{final}}}\right)Δv=Isp​⋅g0​⋅ln(mfinal​minitial​​)
  • Live Flight Operations & Simulation: A real-time Mission Control dashboard simulates 6 flight phases (Ascent →\to→ Separation →\to→ Trans-Injection →\to→ Deep-Space Cruise →\to→ Orbital Insertion →\to→ Science Operations). Live telemetry tracks fuel burn, solar battery buffering, bus temperature, component integrity, and Deep Space Network (DSN) link margin.
  • Dynamic NASA API Integration: The backend queries NASA JPL NeoWs to populate live Near-Earth Asteroid radar feeds (velocity, miss distance, hazardous status) and NASA APOD / Image Library to project high-resolution target imagery. Procedural anomalies (solar storms, micrometeorites) trigger interactive decision prompts requiring strategic trade-offs between spacecraft survival and scientific yield.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Low Barrier to Entry with High Scientific Fidelity: Unlike dry aerospace tools (e.g., GMAT or Systems Tool Kit) that require specialized training, or arcade games that ignore physics, MissionVerse combines intuitive UI with genuine astrophysics.
  • Experiential STEM Learning: Instead of memorizing equations, players discover the tyranny of the rocket equation firsthand—experiencing why a heavier sensor demands exponentially more propellant.
  • 100% Zero-Configuration Local Execution: Runs smoothly in any modern web browser on consumer laptops without demanding GPU requirements or complex native dependencies.
  • Resilient Architecture: Incorporates intelligent in-memory API caching and graceful fallbacks, ensuring continuous, crash-free operation even when offline or during NASA API rate limits.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Inspiring the Artemis Generation: MissionVerse demystifies astronautics for middle school, high school, and university students, encouraging careers in aerospace engineering and data science.
  • Promoting NASA Open Science: Demonstrates practical, gamified utilization of NASA’s public datasets, showing how open science can create engaging educational software.
  • Global Accessibility: Built as open-source web technology, enabling students in under-resourced schools worldwide to experience high-tier spaceflight simulation for free.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3, Python.
  • Frontend Framework & UI: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Motion (animations), Lucide icons, Three.js / React Three Fiber (3D celestial rendering).
  • State Management: Zustand with local persistent storage for mission blueprints, telemetry logs, and high-score debriefs.
    • NASA NeoWs API: Real-time orbital vectors and physical characteristics of Near-Earth Asteroids.
    • NASA APOD & NASA Image Library API: High-resolution deep-space photography and mission media archives.
    • NASA EPIC API: Full-disc natural color Earth observations from Lagrange Point 1.
    • NASA JPL Solar System Dynamics (SSD): Standard gravitational parameters (μ=GM\mu = GMμ=GM) and planetary orbital radii.
  • Hardware/Environment: Developed and validated on standard Windows laptops running Node.js v24 and Python 3.12.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Live Data as Gameplay Mechanics: Rather than using static mockups, live Near-Earth Asteroids currently orbiting in our solar system appear directly on the player’s radar screen as collision hazards or rendezvous science targets.
  • Tactical Emergency Decision Nodes: Instead of automated pass/fail outcomes, the game pauses during critical space weather events (such as Coronal Mass Ejections) and gives players tactical command directives—such as orienting solar arrays into shadow (safe mode) versus overclocking sensors for a +35%+35\%+35% scientific breakthrough at the expense of hardware wear.
  • Cyberpunk Mission Control Aesthetic: Employs modern glassmorphism, glowing orbital trajectory paths, and dynamic telemetry progress meters that make users feel like genuine Flight Directors seated in NASA Mission Control.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Physical & Engineering Trade-Offs: We prioritized authentic spacecraft trade-offs: mass margins, engine Specific Impulse (IspI_{\text{sp}}Isp​), solar flux degradation with distance squared (1/r21/r^21/r2), and communication latency.
  • Rate Limits & Offline Usability: To prevent the game from failing under NASA's DEMO_KEY rate limit (30 requests/hour), we designed a backend caching layer with fallback telemetry so judging demonstrations remain 100% reliable.
  • Accessibility & Responsiveness: Clean typography, color-coded status badges (nominal, advisory, alert), and responsive layouts ensure clarity across various screen resolutions.
  • Modular Extensibility: Clean component architecture allows future expansions, such as atmospheric Entry, Descent & Landing (EDL) mini-games and classroom multiplayer modes.
